opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as a straight trade-off where we buy more security by spending fewer tokens, or the reverse. They're different axes, and the mistake is letting the token budget conversation crowd out the security one.

On spending, my general view is that coding assistants are some of the highest-leverage tools engineers have right now. If an engineer saves a few hours a week, the token cost is usually small next to their time. So I'd rather not have people rationing usage. What I care about is whether the usage is productive. Are the agents producing code that gets merged, or are they spinning in loops and burning context? That's more an engineering-quality question than a budget one.

Security is the part I'm more opinionated about, because the failure modes are lopsided. Overspending on tokens costs money. A security mistake can leak customer data, and for a data platform that's existential. So a few principles matter a lot.

First, think hard about what the agent can access. These tools are most useful when they have lots of context: your repo, your docs, sometimes your environments. But every bit of access widens the blast radius if something goes wrong, whether that's prompt injection through some file it reads or the agent just doing something dumb. So you want least privilege, sandboxed execution, and a clear line between "reads code" and "touches production or credentials."

Second, governance matters as much as the model. Which models and providers is data going to, what's logged, what's retained? That's the same kind of problem we think about for data and AI governance generally. You want one place where you can see and control it, not every team wiring up its own thing.

Third, keep humans and existing controls in the loop. AI-generated code should go through the same review, testing, and scanning as anything else, maybe more, since it can look very plausible while being subtly wrong.

So the short version: be fairly generous on tokens, because productivity gains usually justify it, and be pretty strict on access and governance, because that's where the real risk is. The worst outcome would be cheaping out on usage while being loose about what the agents can touch. That gives you the downside without the upside.

r001.rationale: The response favors generous token use but does not attribute Databricks’ lower concern relative to consulting firms to having a much smaller coding workforce.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't really treat it as a tradeoff where you dial one up and the other goes down. Token spend on coding agents is, for us, a pretty cheap input compared to what it produces. An engineer's time is far more expensive than the tokens the agent burns, so if an agent runs for a while exploring the codebase, running tests, iterating, that's generally fine. Where we are careful is on what the agent is allowed to touch, not on how many tokens it uses.

So the security side is really about the environment. The agent runs in a sandboxed context with scoped credentials, it can't reach production data or customer workspaces, and anything it produces still goes through the same code review and CI that a human change would. We've also found that a lot of the "security" risk from AI coding is really a review problem. If you let people merge agent output faster than anyone can actually read it, you've changed your risk profile even if the model never did anything malicious. So we've invested in things like automated review passes, tests the agent has to pass, and clear ownership for who signs off.

On cost, what we actually watch is more like cost per merged change, or cost per resolved issue, rather than raw tokens. And we've seen the same thing a lot of our customers see: the first instinct is to cap spend, but the better move is usually to look at where tokens are being wasted. Agents that keep retrying because they don't have the right context, or that re-read the same files over and over. Fixing that with better tooling, better repo documentation, and good retrieval cuts cost more than any budget cap does, and it also tends to make the agent safer, because it's doing fewer blind actions.

The one place I would say we are genuinely conservative is anything that gives the agent the ability to execute against real infrastructure. We'd rather spend more tokens having it reason and simulate than give it a live credential to save a few steps. So if there is a tradeoff, it's that we accept somewhat higher token cost in exchange for a tighter blast radius.

r001.rationale: The response says tokens are cheap relative to engineer time, but does not attribute Databricks’ lower concern to having a smaller coding workforce than large consulting firms.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate those into two questions. Security is a constraint: what code and data can the tool access, where does that information go, and what actions can it take? You want clear boundaries there regardless of how much you spend on tokens.

Then, within those boundaries, the economic question is whether the tool saves engineers time and produces good results. The token bill alone isn’t a great measure. A cheap run that creates hours of debugging can be more expensive than a longer run that gets the task right. So I’d look at cost per successfully completed task, including review and rework, and give people room to experiment within a secure environment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses security and token economics generally, but does not say Databricks is less concerned about spending than large consulting firms or attribute that difference to a smaller coding workforce.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate those into two decisions. Security is a constraint: you need to control what code and data the tools can access, where that information goes, and what actions require review. Spending more or fewer tokens doesn’t change that requirement.

Within those boundaries, I’d look at the economics pretty pragmatically. If a coding assistant uses more tokens but saves an engineer substantial time and produces a change we can validate, that can be a good trade. The metric I’d care about is the cost of getting to a correct, reviewed result, rather than the token bill by itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses security and coding-assistant economics, but does not say Databricks is less concerned about token spending than large consulting firms because it has a smaller coding workforce.
